display.title: Episode 246: The Return of Yehudah, Chapter 5 (Aseres Yemei Teshuvah)
display.summary_short: A show for the Ten Days of Teshuvah: how mitzvos bind us to Hashem, a young yeshiva boy leads the Shema, The Return of Yehudah continues, and why Tashlich is said by running water.
display.summary_long: Broadcast right after Rosh Hashanah 5747, in the Ten Days of Teshuvah. Uncle Yossi explains that the word mitzvah also means 'connection': every mitzvah binds us to Hashem, while an aveirah moves us away, so now is the time for more Torah, davening and tzedakah, and for the joy of a mitzvah. After the first Hakochainik march of the new year, a six-and-a-half-year-old boy from the Lubavitcher Yeshiva leads the Shema in Studio 604. Story time continues The Return of Yehudah: Reb Moshe and Sarah, unable to go back to the pit for little Yehudah without being caught by the cruel poritz, put their trust in Hashem, travel on, and settle in a village where Reb Moshe becomes the melamed, never forgetting their son. Uncle Yossi then explains Yom Kippur and Tashlich: we throw our sins into moving water to show we will never take them back, like a paper that floats away for good. The show ends with a tour of the Tishrei Tzivos Hashem newsletter and its mitzvah missions.
display.lesson: Teshuvah means coming back to Hashem by doing more mitzvos and firmly deciding never to repeat a wrong, and whatever Hashem does is for the good.

date.note: 'We are right after Rosh Hashanah, in the middle of the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah'; Tuesday after Rosh Hashanah 5747, one day after the weekly estimate.

advisories.note: Parents must leave their baby behind in a poritz's pit and travel on without him.
A cruel poritz would put the escaped Jewish family to death if they returned.

privacy.note: The Shema guest gives his full name, age and school; his teacher is named.

sources_cited.note: 'Pikudei Hashem yesharim, mesamchei lev': the mitzvos are straight and gladden the heart.
Rabbi Akiva's 'Kol d'avid Rachmana l'tav avid', quoted by Reb Moshe in the story.
